The tree that gives the place its name is not really a tree but a giant yucca, with spiky green leaves and a twisted, branching trunk. Mormon settlers are said to have named it after the biblical Joshua, seeing the outstretched arms as a gesture of prayer. The trees grow only in the Mojave Desert, and they thrive at this elevation, forming open woodlands that, in spring, burst with creamy white flowers. The surrounding hills are piles of rounded granite boulders, which attract rock climbers from around the world.

Park Boulevard enters the park a short distance from town and runs through the heart of it, across a high plateau of boulders, yuccas and desert scrub, with views of distant ranges. The road is smooth, with long gentle bends and low speed limits, and it passes the Hidden Valley, Jumbo Rocks and the Cholla Cactus Garden, where the spiny plants glow in the low sun. Traffic is heavy in spring and on weekends, and there are cyclists and climbers on the road. Wind can be strong, and dust storms occasionally sweep across the flats.

Fuel is available in Joshua Tree and in the larger town of Yucca Valley, about eleven kilometres away, and it is important to fill up before entering the park, where there are no stations. Cafes and shops line the highway, and the nearby ghost-town-turned-film-set of Pioneertown is a fun detour. Summer temperatures can exceed forty degrees Celsius, so ride in the cool months, from October to May. The night skies are dark and clear, with a dense spread of stars, and the sunrise over the boulders is a good reason to get up early.
t.hidden valley@34.0,-116.2:
Hidden Valley is a small, boulder-ringed basin in Joshua Tree National Park, and it looks, appropriately enough, like a place a person might hide something. Piles of pale monzogranite, rounded by weathering into stacked blocks and domes, form a natural wall around a flat of grass and desert shrubs, with a one-mile loop trail running through it. The local legend says that cattle rustlers used the valley to hide stolen herds in the late nineteenth century, behind rock walls that made a natural corral, and that a rancher named Bill Keys later improved the site for his own cattle. The story is well worn, but the setting makes it easy to believe.

Joshua trees are the star of the park, and here they stand scattered around the boulders, their branches twisted into odd shapes. They are not trees at all, but a kind of yucca, and they only grow in the Mojave Desert. The name is said to have been given by Mormon settlers, who thought the arms reached out like the biblical Joshua. Climbers love this part of the park, and on any weekend morning you will see them bouldering on the rock faces, chalk bags swinging.

Park Boulevard is the road through. It runs north-south through the heart of the park, a smooth, gently rolling ribbon with wide curves, long views and a desert palette of tan and olive. It is not a technical ride, but the combination of boulders, Joshua trees and open sky is remarkable. In spring, if there has been rain, wildflowers cover the ground. Summer is brutally hot, with midday temperatures over forty degrees, so ride early or late, and in winter, mornings can be near freezing.

Twentynine Palms, about seventeen kilometres to the north, is the nearest sizeable town, with fuel, supermarkets and restaurants, and the town of Joshua Tree, on the west side, has more cafes and shops. A park entrance fee is charged, and the car park at Hidden Valley is small, so come early. Carry plenty of water, wear a hat, and leave the cacti alone. The silence here is one of the best things about the place.
t.keys view@33.9,-116.2:
Keys View sits on the crest of the Little San Bernardino Mountains at about 1,580 metres, and the view from it is the longest in Joshua Tree National Park. Below you the land falls away sharply into the Coachella Valley, a broad, flat basin of date palms, golf courses and spreading towns, with Palm Springs on the near side and the Salton Sea glinting far off to the south on a clear day. Beyond lie the high peaks of the San Jacinto and San Gorgonio mountains, snow-capped for much of the winter.

The drop beneath your feet is not an accident. The long, straight line at the foot of the mountains is the San Andreas Fault, the great crack in the earth where the Pacific and North American plates grind slowly past each other. You can see the line of the fault from the viewpoint, a dark stripe of vegetation where the water collects. The valley is a rift, and the mountains are on the move, though at the pace of a fingernail growing. The viewpoint takes its name from Bill Keys, a homesteader who ran a ranch, a mill and a family in the park for decades.

The road to Keys View is a spur off Park Boulevard, climbing about five miles from Park Boulevard in easy bends through juniper and yucca. It is a quiet, well-surfaced road, with short climbs and a clear view ahead, and a good ride on any bike. Haze can obscure the view, particularly in summer, because smog from the Los Angeles basin drifts in from the west. The best time is after a storm, in winter or early spring, when the air is crisp and the mountains stand out sharp. The wind at the top can be fierce, and the temperature several degrees cooler than at the desert floor.

There are no services at Keys View, only a car park, toilets and a short paved path to the viewpoint. Carry water and warm layers, because it can be breezy even on a hot day. Sunset is the favourite hour, when the valley lights come on.
t.cholla cactus garden@33.9,-115.9:
The Cholla Cactus Garden is the sort of place that makes you slow down on instinct. Over a flat expanse of the Pinto Basin, thousands of teddy bear cholla stand in dense, silvery stands, each one a spiny cluster of jointed stems that glows with a golden halo when the light hits it from behind. They look soft, which is the trap. The spines are barbed, the joints detach at a touch, and anyone who has met one will tell you it does not feel cuddly. A short loop trail winds through the thickest part, and you should stay on it.

The garden belongs to the Colorado Desert, the lower and hotter part of the park, where the vegetation is more sparse and the colours more muted than the Joshua trees farther up. Ocotillo, creosote bush and smoke trees dot the washes, and after a wet winter the whole area bursts into bloom in March and April. The best time to visit is in the late afternoon, when the low sun lights the spines and the heat has eased. Sunrise is also magnificent, and quiet.

The ride in is part of the pleasure. Park Boulevard descends from the high Mojave plateau through a long, easy sweep of curves, and as you drop in altitude the air warms and the landscape changes. The road is smooth, with long straights and good visibility, and the traffic is light on weekdays. This is a place where the sky is enormous, and in summer it is also fierce, with midday heat close to fifty degrees on the tarmac, so riding in the early morning or evening is much more comfortable. Watch for wildlife, particularly at dusk, and for loose sand blown across the road.

There is no water or fuel at the garden, only a small car park and a trail. The nearest towns are Twentynine Palms, about twenty-six kilometres away, which has petrol, shops and cafes, and Indio, to the south, which is bigger. Fill up before entering the park, because distances are long and signal is patchy. Bring water, wear a hat, and keep children and pets well away from the plants. If you do get a spine in you, a comb or pair of pliers is the way to remove it.
t.cottonwood spring@33.7,-115.8:
Cottonwood Spring is an oasis in the lower corner of Joshua Tree National Park, where the high Mojave desert gives way to the hotter Colorado Desert, and a small cluster of fan palms and cottonwood trees grows around a spring that has been used for centuries. The Cahuilla people gathered here, grinding seeds and mesquite beans in rock mortars, and the holes can still be seen in the boulders. Later, gold miners camped by the water, and ruins of their mills survive in the hills.

The spring itself is a modest affair, but in a landscape this dry, a patch of shade and a trickle of water are very valuable. Birds come in, from migrating warblers to roadrunners, and bighorn sheep sometimes drink in the early morning. The surroundings are low, open desert of creosote bush, ocotillo and cholla, and in good years in spring, wildflowers cover the ground in yellow, purple and white. A short trail leads to Mastodon Peak, a rocky hill with views over the valley and the old mine workings.

The ride south from the main part of the park is a long, gentle descent, from the stands of Joshua trees through a sloping desert of boulders and into a wide, sandy basin, with the Pinto Basin on one side and the Eagle Mountains rising on the other. The road is smooth, quiet and flowing, with long straights, and it takes you from one ecosystem to another, with the temperature climbing as you drop. At the end, you reach the interstate, and the sudden rush of traffic feels harsh after the silence.

Mecca, to the south, has more services. Summer heat is severe, so ride early, wear light gear and carry plenty of water. The best months are from late October to April, and the night sky is magnificent.
t.santa monica pier@34.0,-118.5:
The longest road in American mythology runs out of land here. Route 66 was commissioned in 1926 to link Chicago with Los Angeles, and as it went through eight states on its two-thousand-mile journey it picked up the nickname the Mother Road. The official end of the highway is a matter of fine print, with the route having been rerouted several times, but the pier at Santa Monica carries a sign calling it the End of the Trail, and that is where riders photograph their bikes, so that is where this ride finishes.

The pier itself opened in 1909 and has been a seaside amusement ever since, with a carousel from the 1920s, an amusement park with a solar-powered Ferris wheel, arcades, fishing from the rails, and the sound of gulls and the hiss of surf beneath the boards. It has been repaired and rebuilt after storms and fires. The Pacific stretches out to the horizon, and on a clear evening the sun sets in a long orange ribbon over the water, while the mountains of Malibu line the coast to the north.

Route 66 was decommissioned in 1985, replaced by the interstates, but Americans refused to let it go, and the old road, in pieces, has become a pilgrimage. Reaching this point after a long trip across the desert is a reward in itself. The last miles through Los Angeles are slow and urban, with traffic lights, lane splitting by locals, and a lot of cars, so choose your hours carefully. Rush hours can be dense, and the best time to arrive is in the late morning or the evening.

Everything you need is here, including fuel, though prices in California are among the highest in the country. Parking for motorcycles near the pier is easier than for cars, but there are fees and rules, so look at the signs. The Venice boardwalk, with its muscle gym, skate park and street performers, is a short ride south. Fresh seafood and tacos are easy to find, and in summer, the marine layer can bring cool grey mornings, so a light jacket is welcome. The beach is wide, and the Pacific is cold, even in August.
t.cova de la catxupa abric i@38.8,0.1:
The Marina Alta is the northern Costa Blanca at its most mixed: villas on every slope, a ribbon of coast running from Moraira to Jávea, and just behind it, farm terraces, dry stone walls and small rock shelters where prehistoric people left their mark. The Cova de la Catxupa, near Teulada and Benitachell, is one of them, a shelter in the hills a few kilometres from the sea, listed with the other Mediterranean rock art of the Iberian Peninsula.

Teulada is the inland twin of the resort of Moraira, an old village of white houses with a fortified church at its heart. Across the hills, Gata de Gorgos is known for two crafts: guitar making, with several workshops building Spanish guitars, and weaving of palm and cane into baskets, hats and furniture, sold in shops along the main road. Benitachell sits below the headland of the Cumbre del Sol, with cliffs dropping straight into the sea.

The Marina Alta was once raisin country. Moscatel grapes were dried in the sun and under riuraus, long arched porches attached to farmhouses, and many of them survive. The wine and the mistela, a sweet fortified drink, are still made, and the farmhouses are a lovely sight in the landscape. The light here is bright, the sea glitters in the distance, and in late winter the almond blossom paints the valleys pink and white.

Riding here is mixed. The coastal roads are busy, particularly in summer, and urbanisations mean frequent junctions, roundabouts and slow traffic. But head a few kilometres inland and the roads become quieter, climbing into the hills with good bends and views back to the coast. The roads toward Jalón and the Vall de Pop, and the climbs into the mountains behind, are well loved by local riders.

Teulada is a town of nearly fifteen thousand with fuel and services, and Gata de Gorgos has everything you need too. Moraira and Jávea offer seafood restaurants, beaches and cafés, and the area is lively all year round thanks to the many foreign residents.
t.c5 area between the ravines of torrevell:
Menorca is a gentler island than its neighbours, and the Talaiotic culture left behind a remarkable landscape of stone monuments that UNESCO recognised in 2023. These are the talaiots, round or square towers of dry stone, the taulas, great T-shaped stone altars, and the navetas, boat-shaped tombs, all dating from the second and first millennia BC. Nobody knows exactly what the people who built them believed, but the sheer number is astonishing for an island that you can cross by car in an hour. C5 is one of the numbered zones of that heritage landscape, in the area between the ravines of Torrevella, south of Alaior.

The land here is low, open and windswept, a patchwork of small fields divided by dry stone walls, and the walls themselves are an old craft, still repaired by hand. Holm oaks and wild olives stand in clumps, and the soil is red and stony. The famous north wind, the tramontana, can blow for days and bend the trees into permanent leaning shapes. The smell in summer is of hot stone and thyme, and in the evening the light on the walls is gold. Menorca is a UNESCO biosphere reserve, and its quieter roads and bridleways make it a place for slow travel.

The riding is simple and pleasant. The island's main road runs along the spine from Maó to Ciutadella, and smaller roads branch off to farms and coves with a mix of gentle curves and straights, tight stone walls on either side. Speeds are low and traffic can be thick in July and August, with hire cars and cyclists. The surface is generally good, though minor roads can be narrow and rough, and tourist coaches need patience.

Alaior, about five kilometres away, is a sizeable town of eight and a half thousand with fuel, supermarkets and a good market. It is also known for its cheese, a mild, slightly salty cow's milk cheese that has its own protected name, and for its ice cream. Spring is the best season, with wildflowers and warm days, and September is calm and warm after the crowds have left. Winter can be wet and windy, and some places close.
Menorca is the quiet island of the Balearics, and its south coast is cut by ravines, the barrancs, that run down from the limestone plateau to the sea in narrow, green clefts. The central-south area is where they are most impressive: Algendar, Trebalúger, Binigaus and others, each a steep-sided channel with wild olive, holm oak and a trickle of water in the bottom, ending in a small beach. The whole island was declared a Biosphere Reserve in 1993, and the old walking path that circles it, the Camí de Cavalls, passes by the mouths of most of them.

Getting here by motorcycle is simple but slow. The island has one main road running along its spine from Maó to Ciutadella, and from it small lanes drop toward the coast between dry stone walls, in a pattern that has hardly changed for centuries. Those lanes are narrow, often with blind corners and the occasional tractor, and speed limits are low and enforced. The north wind, the Tramuntana, can blow hard in winter and spring, so check the forecast before you set out. Summer brings crowds and heat, while May, June and late September are the sweet spots for a quiet ride.

Alaior, seven kilometres off, has nearly nine thousand people and is where you buy fuel and food. It is the home of the island's cheese, a soft, tangy variety with a protected name that comes in square blocks. Ferreries, with over four thousand, is another handy town. The island also holds an extraordinary Bronze Age legacy in its stone talayots and taulas, towers and T-shaped monuments built over three thousand years ago, now recognised by UNESCO, and many of them stand beside the very roads you ride.

Try the local gin, flavoured with juniper and made on the island since the British period in the eighteenth century, when the Royal Navy was stationed at Maó. Menorcans also claim, with some conviction, that mayonnaise was born in Maó. Whether or not that is true, a plate of grilled fish with a dollop of it on a terrace above a barranc is a very good way to end a day.
t.cova de la catxupa abric ii@38.8,0.1:
Teulada is the town, and Moraira is its seaside annexe, and between them they hold most of what people know about this slice of the Costa Blanca. The Catxupa shelter lies just outside the town, which has some fourteen and a half thousand residents, many of them northern Europeans who came for the sun and stayed. The old centre of Teulada, though, remains a Valencian one, with a fortified parish church and narrow lanes that fill with the smell of coffee and baking at midday.

The second shelter in the Catxupa group is a small overhang under the limestone slopes that fall toward the sea. The Levantine tradition of painting in red on rock shelters is found all along this coast, and this is one of the closer ones to the sea. It is a reminder that before holidaymakers, before the Romans and Moors, these slopes were hunting country, with the coast visible from the hills and game running through the scrub.

Moraira, a short ride down the hill, is the charming part. It is a former fishing village with a little castle on the point, built in the eighteenth century to guard against raiders from the sea, and a beach protected by a rocky headland. The nearby cape of Cap d'Or is a dramatic spit of land that looks like a dragon's back, and the cliffs near the Cap de la Nau, to the north, are among the finest on this coast. Moscatel grapes grow on the terraces, and the sweet wine made from them is worth a bottle.

The riding is a mix of gentle coastal bends and quick climbs inland. Roads here are good and mostly well maintained, though the traffic can be heavy in July and August, when everyone is trying to reach the beach. If you want peace, come in spring or autumn, or go inland by the back roads toward Benissa and Xàbia, which are quieter and more scenic.

Teulada has pumps, supermarkets, cafés and restaurants, so fuel and lunch are no trouble. Bring water for the walk to the shelter.
t.cova de la catxupa abric iii@38.8,0.1:
Behind Teulada the land rises sharply, and the third shelter in the Catxupa series sits where the first foothills begin. It is not an obvious place for an ancient painted site. The coast is only a few kilometres away, and the view toward the sea is partly built over. But the Levantine rock art tradition ran right down to this edge of the Mediterranean, and the overhangs of the hills here were used by people long before anyone built a villa.

Think of it as a gateway. A few minutes inland from Teulada the road starts climbing, and within half an hour you are in a landscape of terraces, almond trees and narrow lanes more typical of the Marina Alta interior. The Coll de Rates is the great local climb, a pass of around six hundred metres on the road between Parcent and Tàrbena, and it is a favourite with cyclists and motorcyclists alike. From the top the view back toward the Mediterranean is worth the hairpins, and a bar there serves a decent coffee and a plate of olives.

The area is also known for its wine. Moscatel de Alejandría, the sweet muscat grape, thrives on these slopes, and the villages of the Jalón valley make a wine that tastes of raisins and orange peel. Raisins are still dried in sheds called riurau, open-fronted porches that you will spot on farms beside the road, a tradition that dates back to the Moors.

Roads on this side of the hills are twisty and sometimes narrow, with surfaces that vary. Traffic is light on weekdays, but on Sundays you will share the bends with cyclists, so keep your speed sensible. In summer the middle of the day can be punishing, and in winter the mountains can be cold and damp. Autumn is the best season, with warm days and clear air.

Teulada is only three kilometres away and has everything you need: fuel, cafés, supermarkets. Carry water, as the shelters have none.
t.imperial tombs of the ming and qing dyna:
Long before the Manchus took Beijing, they had a home, and it was in the green, hilly country east of Shenyang, where the Hun river comes out of the Changbai foothills. Yongling, the Qing dynasty's earliest imperial tomb, stands there in the county of Xinbin, built at the start of the seventeenth century and expanded afterwards to house the ancestors of Nurhaci, the chief who united the Jurchen tribes and founded the line that would rule China until 1912. It is an old-fashioned ceremonial complex, with walls, a stone bridge, spirit-way sculptures and a tomb mound behind, set against a wooded hillside, and it makes a clear point: before they were emperors of China, these people were mountain chieftains.

The tomb belongs, with the Ming tombs near Beijing and other Qing tombs in Shenyang and Hebei, to the World Heritage group of the imperial tombs of the Ming and Qing dynasties. The ride also takes in Wunu Mountain City, a mountain fortress built by the earlier kingdom of Goguryeo, a thousand years before the Manchu era, high on a flat-topped cliff near Huanren. Together the two give a picture of how this north-eastern borderland has always been a place where powers met.

I should be honest about the riding. Taking a foreign motorcycle across China requires permits, a guide and temporary licences, and few visitors manage it independently, so most riders here will use a local rental or a tour. The reward, for those who do, is a countryside of forested hills, maize and rice fields, small Manchu villages and winding river roads, with the whole area beautifully red and gold in October. Summers are green and humid, and winters are bitterly cold, with snow and ice, so the best months are May, June and September.

Fushun, the nearest big city, is an old coal and industrial town, and Xinbin has a few fuel stations and restaurants of its own, but facilities thin out in the hills, so fill the tank when you can. Northeastern Chinese cooking is hearty: pork stewed with pickled cabbage, dumplings with thick wrappers, and river fish from the mountain streams, washed down with a local beer. In the villages, drying corn hangs in golden strings from the eaves, a bright detail on a grey autumn day.
t.malibu@34.0,-118.8:
Twenty-one miles of the Pacific Coast Highway pass through Malibu, and most of them are within sight of the sea. The road squeezes between the steep brown slopes of the Santa Monica Mountains and a narrow ribbon of sand, a mix of beach houses, small plazas, surf breaks and sudden gaps with a view over the water. The town itself has about thirteen thousand people, a city of film stars and surfers, and a strong feeling of being at the edge of something. It was once a ranch owned by the Rindge family, who held off development for decades, and the land was divided only in the 1920s, after the state forced a public road through it.

The highway is famous, and for good reason, but it is not a race track. At weekends the road fills with sightseers, delivery vans, cyclists and drivers looking for a place to park, and there are speed limits, traffic lights and patrols, with fines that are not small. The coast road has had a bad record for crashes. A good plan is to go early on a weekday, when the light comes slanting over the hills and the sea is pale blue, and the road is almost clear. In late spring and early summer the morning fog, called June gloom, can sit over the shore until noon.

For something with more bends, take one of the canyon roads that climb into the mountains. Malibu Canyon Road, Decker, Latigo and Mulholland Highway all twist up through chaparral and oak, with drops, cambers and tight corners that reward a rider with some care, and with the sea sparkling far below as you climb. They are narrow, and the surface can be rough, with gravel and fallen rock, and in places there are no barriers. Fires have swept through the mountains repeatedly, including the Woolsey fire of 2018 and the Palisades fire of 2025, leaving scars on the hills and homes, so you will see burned areas and rebuilding. Check the road status in fire season and after heavy rain, when landslides can close sections.

Fuel in Malibu is among the most expensive in California, so fill up in Santa Monica or Oxnard if you can, though there are stations along the highway. For a break, a beach cafe or a fish shack near the pier serves tacos and clam chowder with a view. The Getty Villa, a museum of ancient art in a replica Roman villa, lies a few miles south and is free to enter, with booking.
t.natural site@38.8,1.4:
If the pin is where I think it is, it sits on the southern tip of Ibiza, among the salt pans and pinewoods of Ses Salines, which means the label Natural Site is quite literal. This is the end of the island where the beach clubs thin out and the landscape opens up into flat white salt flats, a lagoon full of flamingos in winter and spring, and a long beach called Es Cavallet where the dunes hold their shape. The coordinates are only approximate, so I would treat the stop as a visit to the park rather than a single spot.

The salt is the clue to the island's history. Phoenician settlers arrived about the eighth century BC and founded a trading settlement, and the pans have been worked ever since, with Carthaginians, Romans, Moors and Catalans all taking their share. The salt was one of Ibiza's reasons for existing, and it is why the town, Dalt Vila, its fortified old quarter, and the Puig des Molins necropolis, a great Phoenician and Punic cemetery on the edge of the city, are now part of a UNESCO site that also includes the sea-grass meadows around the island. The Posidonia, a flowering plant that grows in vast underwater fields, keeps the water here clear and turquoise.

For riding, Ibiza is better than its reputation. The roads are small, tarred and fairly empty outside high season. The route south from Ibiza town towards Sant Josep passes through pine, fig and carob groves, with red earth and low stone walls, and the road along the salt pans is flat, open and breezy. In July and August traffic is heavy and the car parks fill, so aim for May, June or late September, when the water is warm and the light is gentle.

Ibiza town, thirteen kilometres away, has everything in the way of fuel, food and rooms, and Sant Josep, a little closer, has a few pumps. The island has no great mountains, though Sa Talaia reaches about 475 metres, and you can see Formentera across the strait on a clear day.
t.ventura@34.3,-119.2:
Ventura is a laid-back beach city on the coast of Southern California, and the pin sits in the middle of it, with the old mission, the pier and the long curve of Highway 101 beside the sea. Mission San Buenaventura, founded in 1782 by Father Junípero Serra, was the last of the missions he established, and its church and garden are a quiet, peaceful corner in the middle of the town. Ventura Pier, built in 1872, is the longest wooden pier in California, a long wooden promenade that pokes out into the Pacific, and fishermen and walkers stroll along it.

The sea here is rich and the weather is mild. The Channel Islands, a group of rugged islands that form a national park, lie about thirty kilometres offshore, and boats leave from Ventura Harbor to carry visitors to them. On the way you may see dolphins, whales and seabirds. To the north, the road follows the coast through Rincon, a famous surf break, with the ocean on one side and the cliffs on the other, and the highway runs under the shadow of the Santa Ynez mountains. Inland, Highway 33 leads up the Ventura river valley to Ojai, a little town with orange groves and an arts scene.

The riding is of two kinds. The coastal run on Highway 101 is fast, wide and busy, with beautiful views of the sea and the islands, and it is a fine way to get north to Santa Barbara, but the traffic can be dense, especially at weekends. The inland roads, particularly Highway 33 and the smaller roads in the hills, are tighter, with curves, climbs and wide vistas of orange and avocado groves. The surface is generally good, though sections are rough, and in autumn the Santa Ana winds can be strong and hot.

Fuel, food and coffee are easy, with Ventura offering every service, and the old downtown has a good selection of cafés, restaurants and breweries. Fish tacos and fresh seafood are staples, and a coffee on the pier in the morning is a good start. Try an avocado, as the area is a big producer.

Walk to the end of the pier at sunset. The sky turns orange, the islands become shadows, and the sea is calm. It is the very picture of the California coast.
Agoura Hills lies at the northern foot of the Santa Monica Mountains, where the suburban sprawl of the San Fernando Valley runs out into oak savanna and sandstone outcrops, and it is a natural stopping point for anyone riding the canyons to the sea. With over twenty thousand people, the town has all the fuel and food you could want, and nearby Westlake Village has a lake and more restaurants. This is the place to fill the tank and have a proper breakfast before the twisting begins.

The roads that matter here are Mulholland Highway, Malibu Canyon and Kanan Dume Road. Mulholland Highway, named for the engineer who brought the Owens River water to Los Angeles, winds along the crest of the mountains in a series of bends that are tight, fast and well loved by sport riders. The Rock Store, a roadside café at Cornell, has been a gathering place for motorcyclists for decades, and on a Sunday morning it is a loud, colourful scene of chrome and leather. Malibu Canyon drops to the Pacific Coast Highway through a narrow gorge of volcanic rock, passing the state park where the film and television series M*A*S*H was shot.

The mountains here are Chumash country, and the sandstone and chaparral hills hold a surprising range of wildlife, from mule deer and coyotes to the occasional bobcat. In spring the hills are green and wildflowers bloom along the road, but by summer they turn brown and the fire danger is high. Fires have closed these roads in recent years, so check conditions in dry weather.

Be careful on these roads. They are popular with riders, which means they are also popular with the highway patrol, and speed limits are enforced with real enthusiasm. Rock falls, gravel in corners and cars cutting across the line are common hazards, and fatal accidents are frequent. Go early on weekdays if you want the road to yourself. At weekends the best strategy is to arrive at dawn, enjoy the empty bends and be at the Rock Store by eight, when the crowd arrives and the coffee is hot.
t.death valley weekend photo pull off@34.4:
Acton is a high-desert town on the Sierra Highway, where Los Angeles County stops pretending to be a city and starts being the Mojave. The coordinates sit just outside it, on the long slope between the San Gabriel Mountains and the Antelope Valley, and the ride they belong to is the long road to Death Valley, which lies a good four hours north-east. This is the sort of place you reach before breakfast, with the sun just clearing the ridges and a chill still in the sage.

The landmark nearby is Vasquez Rocks, a field of tilted sandstone slabs that jut from the hillside at a steep angle, thrown up by movement along the San Andreas system and worn into blades and fins. The corners are gentle, speeds are low and traffic can be heavy, particularly on summer weekends, so patience is the main skill. Fog in May and June can persist well into the afternoon and is locally known as May Gray and June Gloom.

Just inland is San Juan Capistrano, about five kilometres away, with the old Spanish mission founded in 1776, its ruined stone church and its gardens. The swallows that nest there are said to return each year on the nineteenth of March, St Joseph's Day, and the town still holds a festival. It is worth a short detour from the coast for the quiet courtyards.

Fuel and food are no issue. Stations line the highway, and the harbour has plenty of fish tacos and clam chowder, along with cafes where riders gather on weekend mornings. Parking for motorcycles is usually easy at the harbour and at the state beaches. Doheny State Beach, just north of the harbour, is a long stretch of sand where surfers have been riding the small, steady waves for generations. In winter, grey whales pass offshore on their migration south, and you may see them from the headland with a good pair of binoculars.

Start early, ride north with the ocean on your left and take your time.
t.shitiping@23.5,121.5:
Shitiping means roughly stone steps terrace, and that already tells you a lot about the place. It sits on Taiwan's east coast, where the Coastal Mountain Range drops almost straight into the Pacific, and the highway squeezes itself between rock and sea. The area belongs to the long, wild stretch of Provincial Highway 11, the road that runs south from Hualien towards Taitung with the ocean on one side nearly all the way.

This is among the great motorcycle roads of the island. The surface is generally good, the bends are open and flowing, and the sea view is constant: a deep Pacific blue in the morning, turning silver-grey under cloud. There are tunnels and cuttings, a few tight spots at the headlands and a lot of rolling coastal tarmac where you can settle into a rhythm. Traffic is mostly local trucks, scooters and cyclists, the last of whom come here for exactly the same reason you do. Be careful in typhoon season, from roughly July to October, when rain and rockfall can close sections, and take extra care on wet days, as the paint on the road can be slick.

The geology deserves a look. The rocks along this coast are the result of the Philippine Sea plate colliding with the Eurasian plate, and the cliffs and terraced stone platforms at Shitiping show it, with layered rock shaped by waves and the long push of the tectonic squeeze. People walk the stepped rock shelf at low tide, watching crabs and small tide pools, and the roar of surf on black stone is a good reason to stop and switch off the engine. The coast was also home to Amis communities, an Indigenous people whose fishing and harvest culture is still alive in the villages here, and in summer you might come across festival preparations.

For practical purposes, I do not know of any services at the exact spot, so fill your tank at a larger place in advance. Fuel stations are spaced out along the coast, mostly in the small towns, and it is wise never to push your range. Convenience stores, found in nearly every village, sell cold drinks and simple food, and they are a good place for a rest.
t.mausoleum kbor er roumia@36.6,2.6:
On a low hill west of Algiers, above the farmland of the Mitidja plain and within sight of the sea, stands a great round tomb of pale stone that the French called the Tombeau de la Chrétienne and the Algerians call Kbor er Roumia, the tomb of the Christian woman. The name is a folk memory rather than a fact, since the monument was built in the first century BC for the Berber king Juba II of Mauretania and his wife Cleopatra Selene, the daughter of Mark Antony and Cleopatra of Egypt. A royal couple with that parentage, ruling a Roman client kingdom from the coast of Africa, is a story that sounds invented but is simply true.

The tomb is a drum about sixty metres across, topped by a stepped cone, and it once stood much higher than it does today. Its walls are lined with false Ionic columns, and four false doors mark the cardinal points, a mixture of Numidian, Egyptian and Greek styles that reflects the cosmopolitan taste of the kingdom. Inside, a long spiral corridor leads to the burial chamber, which was robbed in antiquity, and legends of hidden treasure have sent explorers into it for centuries. UNESCO listed it in 1982 together with the nearby ruins of Tipasa, which lies a short way along the coast.

Riding in this part of Algeria is a matter of attention. The roads in the Sahel hills and Mitidja are busy with trucks, minibuses and farm vehicles, the surfaces vary from good to broken, and drivers can be unpredictable, so expect to ride defensively. Police and gendarmerie checkpoints are common on the main routes; keep your passport, licence and vehicle papers to hand, and stay patient and polite. The scenery rewards the effort, with orange groves, vineyards on the slopes and, on a clear day, the blue of the Mediterranean to the north.

The nearest towns are Tipasa, about ten kilometres away, and Hadjout and El Affroun, both bigger, so go there for fuel and food. Fuel in Algeria is inexpensive and widely available in towns, though on country roads it is wise to top up when you see a station. The best time of year is spring or autumn, when the days are warm but not harsh, and the hills are green. In the summer heat the stone glows white and the smell of dry grass and wild thyme fills the air. Stand at the foot of the tomb at dusk and the scale of it begins to sink in.
Tipasa is the kind of ruin that gives you the sea in one direction and the mountain in the other. A Phoenician trading post on this stretch of the Algerian coast became a Roman colony in the first century, and by the later empire it was a prosperous town with a harbour, a forum, villas and, when the city turned Christian, several large basilicas. The remains spread along a rocky shore, among pines, wild fennel and cactus, with the dark mass of the Chenoua mountain rising behind. In the western park you walk among foundations, mosaics and column stumps with the surf rolling in beside you.

The writer Albert Camus, who grew up in Algiers, wrote one of his best-known essays about the place, Nuptials at Tipasa, in which the ruins are overgrown by wild flowers and the stones are warm to the touch. Many visitors say that nothing has changed. The site was inscribed by UNESCO in 1982 for its mixture of Punic, Roman, early Christian and Byzantine remains, and it sits only a short drive from the capital, which makes it a classic day trip for Algerians as well as foreigners.

For a motorcyclist, the coast road from Algiers to Tipasa is one of the pleasantest in the country, with a series of gentle bends between hills, a sparkling sea and a lot of weekend traffic. Expect trucks, buses and cars that overtake without warning, uneven surfaces in places and occasional checkpoints. The best time is early in the day, when the light is clear and the roads are quieter. In summer the beaches fill up, and the parking near the site can be tight. A hat and water are essential; shade is scarce among the stones.

Tipasa town, with about twenty-five thousand people, has fuel stations, small restaurants and cafes serving grilled fish and mint tea, and a sea-view terrace is a fine place for a rest. Hadjout, further inland, is a bigger market town. The air smells of salt, pine resin and the warm herbs of the maquis, and the sound of cicadas fills the afternoon. The ruins are quiet enough to hear your own footsteps on the old paving, and the sunset over the Chenoua is a very good reason to linger.
t.c6 south east area alaior@39.9,4.2:
Menorca has more prehistoric monuments per square kilometre than almost anywhere in Europe, and the land around Alaior is one of the richest parts. In the second millennium BC the island's people, known as the Talayotic culture, built big stone towers called talaiots, sanctuaries with T-shaped stone pillars called taulas, and cave burials, all from huge blocks of limestone piled without mortar. UNESCO inscribed the Talayotic Menorca sites in 2023. Near Alaior, large settlements such as Torre d'en Galmés and Torralba d'en Salord are the best known, and their stone enclosures are scattered across open fields, with dry-stone walls in all directions.

Alaior itself is a white-walled inland town of about nine thousand people on a hill, between Maó and Ciutadella, and it has two claims to fame: cheese and shoes. Mahón cheese, with its protected designation of origin, is produced on farms and in dairies around the town, and the local cheesemakers will happily sell you a wedge. The town has also been a centre for footwear production for generations. There is a lively market, a pleasant plaza and a church to see if it is open.

The riding on Menorca is a pleasant, gentle kind. Roads cross the island in long, rolling lines between stone walls, fields of grass and low olive and wild olive trees, with views toward the sea from the higher spots, and traffic is light outside the summer season. Corners are mild, and the main road, which runs the length of the island, is straight and fast. The northern wind, the Tramuntana, can be strong and salty, and gusts across the open land may push a motorcycle around, so keep a firm grip. Summer brings heat and crowds to the coast, whereas spring and autumn are quiet.

Alaior has fuel stations and supermarkets, and Maó, about nine kilometres away, has everything else, including a big natural harbour and gin made from juniper, a local tradition from the days of the British garrison in the eighteenth century. The Camí de Cavalls, an old coastal path, runs around the island, and many stretches can be reached by small roads. The air smells of thyme, sea spray and warm stone, and the light is bright and clear. Take your time at the monuments, because the stones are best understood in silence.
t.necropolis puig des molins@38.9,1.4:
The hill of Puig des Molins, the hill of the windmills, rises on the edge of Ibiza Town, and under its slopes lies one of the biggest ancient cemeteries in the western Mediterranean. The Phoenicians and then the Carthaginians, who founded the city of Ebusus on this coast in the seventh century BC, buried their dead here for centuries, cutting underground chambers into the soft rock, and they are known as hypogea. Over three thousand of these tombs have been found, and the city's archaeological museum, set at the top of the hill, displays the grave goods that came out of them, including pottery, jewellery, glass beads, terracotta figurines and amulets that came from as far away as Egypt.

The necropolis forms part of the UNESCO World Heritage site listed in 1999, which recognises Ibiza's biodiversity and culture together, along with the walled upper town, the Dalt Vila, and the seagrass meadows offshore. Phoenician Ebusus was a trading post of some importance, and the island was a stop on the sea routes between the Levant, North Africa and the Iberian coast. Among the finds are terracotta figures of the goddess Tanit, who was a major deity of the Punic world, with a beautiful and slightly stern face. The dead were buried with the things they would need, so the tombs are a kind of time capsule.

Ibiza has a reputation for clubs and parties, but the part of the island that matters to a rider is quieter. Roads cross the interior through pine woods, almond and fig groves and terraced fields, with white farmhouses and little churches, and the north coast has twisty roads with sea views. The summer traffic around the town and the airport is dense, so go early or choose spring and autumn, when the island belongs to its inhabitants again. The surface is generally good, but narrow lanes and blind bends call for care, and the wind can be strong on the coast.

Ibiza Town has about forty-eight thousand people, so fuel stations, shops and cafes are in good supply. Santa Eulària des Riu and Sant Josep have more on the other roads. The local speciality is bullit de peix, a fish stew served with rice, and flaó, a cheesecake flavoured with mint and anise. The air smells of pine, salt and herbs, and in the evening the light on the old town walls is wonderful. The museum is worth an hour, and the view from the top of the hill over the harbour is worth another.
t.poblado de sa caleta@38.9,1.3:
On a low cliff above the sea on Ibiza's south-west coast stand the foundations of some of the oldest buildings on the island. The Phoenician settlement of sa Caleta was founded around the eighth or seventh century BC, and for about a century it was a small trading post, with rectangular stone houses laid out along narrow streets, a few metres from the water. The inhabitants worked iron, a sign of their sophistication, and traded with the mainland and North Africa. Around 600 to 550 BC the village was abandoned, and its people, it seems, moved to the harbour of Ebusus, which became the main town. UNESCO included the site in its Ibiza listing of 1999.

The spot itself is wild and beautiful, with rocky coast, pines clinging to the clifftop and clear blue-green water below. A walk among the ruins takes only a short time, but the setting is special, and on a calm day you will see only a few other visitors. Not far to the south-west, the strange rock of Es Vedrà rises from the sea, an island that has attracted legends for centuries. The flat salt pans of Ses Salines, to the south-east, have been worked since Phoenician times and are home to flamingos in the cooler months.

The roads in this part of Ibiza are narrow and twisting, with plenty of short climbs, blind bends and little traffic out of season. The surface is good on the main roads, rougher on the small tracks to the coves. In July and August, the island is crowded, and every cove has its queue of cars, so spring, early summer and autumn are better. In the wind, the pines creak and the sea smells of salt and resin, and the light in the late afternoon is warm and golden.

Sant Josep de sa Talaia, the nearest village, has fuel and some shops, and the larger towns of Ibiza and Sant Antoni lie about ten to thirteen kilometres away, with everything you might need. Bring water when you visit the ruins, because there is little shade, and wear shoes with a good grip, as the rocks can be slippery. A swim after your visit is a fine way to cool off, and a plate of grilled fish at one of the beach restaurants is a decent reward.
t.palma@39.6,2.7:
Palma is a city built around a cathedral that looks like a stone cliff. La Seu, as everyone calls it, rises directly above the seafront, a Gothic mass of pale limestone begun in the early fourteenth century by King James II of Mallorca, with a huge rose window and buttresses that seem to leap toward the sea. It took centuries to build, and in the twentieth century the architect Antoni Gaudí was called in to rework the interior, hanging a great canopy above the altar. The reflection of the building in the long pond in front, at dawn, is one of the great sights of the Mediterranean.

Mallorca's capital has been a trading city since Roman times, and the old town is a maze of narrow streets, courtyards and palaces that reward aimless walking. The Castell de Bellver, a round Gothic castle on a pine-covered hill west of the city, gives a fine view of the bay. For breakfast, locals favour the ensaimada, a spiral-shaped pastry dusted with sugar, and the island is also known for sobrasada, a spreadable cured sausage, and for its almond blossom in late winter.

The great attraction for a rider is the Serra de Tramuntana, the mountain range that runs along the north-west coast and was listed by UNESCO in 2011 as a cultural landscape of terraced hillsides, ancient olive trees and stone villages. The road along it, with its endless curves, cliffs and sea views, is among the best motorcycle roads in Europe, though it can be thronged with cyclists, coaches and tourists in spring and summer. The famous road to Sa Calobra, with its hairpin turns, is a favourite, and so are the quieter roads around Valldemossa and Deià. Surface and signs are good. In the high season, the main roads can be slow, so go early, midweek, or in the shoulder months.

Palma has plenty of fuel stations, and the island's size means you are never far from one, though in the mountains they thin out. Es Molinar and the other suburbs on the east side have small harbours with seafood restaurants. In July and August, the heat and crowds are heavy, and spring and autumn are lovely. The air near the seafront smells of salt and diesel, and in the evening the cathedral glows gold. It is a fine place to begin or end a long day.
t.taroko gorge@24.2,121.6:
Taroko Gorge is the great cleft in Taiwan's eastern flank, where the Liwu river has cut through a mass of marble and schist for several million years, and where the mountains rise almost vertically from the Pacific coast to over three thousand metres. The gate at the mouth lies some twenty kilometres north of Hualien, and from there the road follows the river into a gorge so narrow in places that the walls seem to lean together overhead. The marble is grey, white and streaked, the water is a vivid turquoise, and the sound of the river echoes off the rock.

The road itself is a feat of engineering. The Central Cross-Island Highway, built between 1956 and 1960, was dug by thousands of workers, many of them veterans of the civil war who had come to Taiwan with the army, and many of them died in the construction. A shrine at the entrance to the gorge, the Eternal Spring Shrine, remembers them, built on a hill over a waterfall. The road passes through tunnels cut in the rock, around the Tunnel of Nine Turns, a cliff path carved at the water's edge, and past the Swallow Grotto, where the birds nest on the cliffs. Further up, the road continues to high mountain passes at over three thousand metres, with cloud forest, cold winds and in winter the chance of snow.

The park is subject to rockfalls, landslides and earthquakes, and the road is closed from time to time. A strong earthquake struck Hualien in April 2024 and damaged parts of the gorge and its roads, and some sections were closed for repairs for a long time, so it is essential to check the current status before travelling. Typhoons between July and October can also close the route, and rain can bring sudden falls of rock. Helmets are not just a legal requirement here, and some operators insist on hard hats for walking trails.

The traffic in the gorge includes tour buses on a narrow road, so go early and ride with care. Hualien City, about twenty-one kilometres away, has fuel, food and every service, and the stations get fewer as you climb. The night market in Hualien serves excellent local snacks, including mochi and wild boar sausage, and is a pleasant way to end a day.
t.derby@-17.3,123.6:
Derby sits on a flat peninsula of mud and mangroves at the edge of King Sound, in the far north-west of Western Australia, and it is where the Gibb River Road starts. The tides here are among the biggest in the country, rising and falling about eleven metres, so the shoreline retreats for hundreds of metres twice a day and the water runs fast and brown. The town is small, with around four thousand people, and it has the dusty, relaxed air of a place that does a bit of everything: cattle, mining services, Aboriginal art and tourism.

A few kilometres out of town stands a very old boab tree known as the Prison Tree, a hollow trunk where, according to local stories, prisoners were held overnight on the way to Derby in the late nineteenth century. Historians debate details, but the tree remains a striking sight. The Mowanjum Aboriginal community nearby has an art centre that is well worth a visit, with work by Wanjina artists whose images of spirit figures stand out in the Kimberley's rock art tradition.

The Gibb River Road was built in the 1960s as a way to move cattle from the stations of the Kimberley to the port at Derby. It runs about 660 kilometres east to Wyndham and Kununurra, and for most of its length it is unsealed gravel with corrugations, creek crossings and long distances between supplies. The dry season, from about May to September, is the only sensible time to ride. In the wet, the road floods and is closed. A rider should carry plenty of water, a spare tube, tools and enough fuel for the long gaps, and tell someone the plan.

Derby has fuel, a supermarket and basic services, and it is the last chance for supplies before the ranges. Roadhouses along the way, such as the one at Mount Barnett, sell fuel and food at remote prices, so budget accordingly. Heat is intense, so start at dawn and rest in the shade at midday.

The gorges are the reward. Windjana Gorge, Tunnel Creek, Bell Gorge and Manning Gorge are all within reach, with cool water, red rock and the occasional freshwater crocodile, so swim only where signs say it is safe.
t.lake louise@51.4,-116.2:
Lake Louise is a lake the colour of milky turquoise, set under a wall of rock and a hanging glacier, and it is one of the most photographed places in Canada. The colour comes from fine rock flour, ground by the glacier and carried into the water, which reflects the blue-green part of the spectrum. At about 1,500 metres, the lake is surrounded by the peaks of the Rockies, with Mount Victoria and the Victoria Glacier at its head, and the old château at the foot, a large hotel that has stood here in various forms since the 1890s. The lake was named for Princess Louise Caroline Alberta, a daughter of Queen Victoria, and the province of Alberta also bears her name.

The way here is the Bow Valley Parkway, the quieter road that runs alongside the Trans-Canada Highway between Banff and Lake Louise for about fifty kilometres. It is a rider's delight if you are in the right frame of mind, because the speed limit is low, the road is narrow and lined with tall spruce, and there are lay-bys for wildlife. Elk, deer, bighorn sheep and the occasional black or grizzly bear all use the corridor. Please keep your distance and never stop to approach an animal. At certain times of year, part of the parkway has seasonal restrictions to protect wildlife, so check with the park before you set off.

Banff National Park charges an entry fee, and you need a pass on your windscreen or, for a bike, carried on you. The weather in the mountains changes fast, with snow possible any month of the year, and high passes and roads can close with little warning. Summer is the busiest time, and the car park at the lake fills very early, so arrive in the morning or in the evening.

Fuel and food are available in the village of Lake Louise, a short distance from the lake, with a petrol station, a grocery and a handful of cafes and restaurants. Prices are higher than in Calgary or Banff, so fill up in Banff if you can.

Beyond the village, the Icefields Parkway continues north toward Jasper, one of the great mountain roads of the world.
t.andratx@39.6,2.4:
Andratx is the south-western gateway to Mallorca's Serra de Tramuntana, the mountain range that runs like a spine along the island's north-western coast, and the start of the Ma-10, the island's most famous road. The town is a quiet inland place of about twelve thousand people, with a church fortified against pirates, narrow lanes and a lively Wednesday market, and the sea is a few kilometres away at Port d'Andratx, a smart harbour lined with restaurants and yachts.

The Tramuntana was added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 2011 as a cultural landscape, because for centuries farmers have shaped the steep slopes into terraces of olive and almond, held up by dry-stone walls, and watered by an ingenious system of channels. The mountains rise to over 1,400 metres, and the coast is a rugged line of cliffs and small coves. The road to the north-east passes the villages of Estellencs and Banyalbufar, whose terraces drop to the sea, and Deià, a village that has long attracted artists and writers. Valldemossa, with its Carthusian monastery, is where Frédéric Chopin and George Sand spent the winter of 1838 and 1839, an unhappy stay that nevertheless produced much of his music.

The Ma-10 is one of the great motorcycle roads of Europe, a ribbon of bends, tunnels and hairpins cut into the slope, with fine views over the Mediterranean. It is also very popular with cyclists, tour buses and rental cars, particularly in spring and summer, and overtaking is difficult. Surface is generally good, though some stretches are rough, and the road is narrow, with a few tight tunnels. In winter and early spring, it is much quieter, and the light on the sea is very clear.

Fuel is easy in Andratx and Port d'Andratx, and less so on the mountain road, so fill up before leaving. Cafes and restaurants line the harbour, serving fresh fish, paella and the local ensaïmada pastry. Camp de Mar, a small resort a few kilometres away, has a sheltered beach.

The best months for riding are April, May, June, September and October, when the days are mild and the crowds thinner.
t.mulholland and@34.2,-118.0:
The pin lies on the lower slopes of the San Gabriel Mountains, near Sierra Madre and Arcadia, at the place where the Los Angeles basin runs right up against the mountains. Behind the neat grid of streets, the mountain wall rises steeply, thick with chaparral, and in clear weather after rain it is covered with a dusting of snow at the top, which surprises visitors who associate the city only with beaches.

Sierra Madre is a small foothill town that prides itself on its village feel, with a pleasant main street, old bungalows and a long shadow of the mountain across it in the late afternoon. It is famous for its wisteria vine, planted in 1894 and said to be the largest blossoming plant in the world, which bursts into bloom in March and draws crowds. Arcadia, lower down, is home to Santa Anita Park, an Art Deco horse-racing track from the 1930s with the mountains as a backdrop, and the nearby arboretum has peacocks wandering the lawns.

For motorcyclists, the mountain above is the draw. Mount Wilson Road climbs to the observatory on the summit, where a century ago astronomers used a large telescope to show that the universe contained other galaxies, which changed how we understand the cosmos. The road to the top is narrow, steep and quite twisty, and it is shared with hikers and cyclists. Angeles Crest Highway, a little to the west, is the main attraction, a long, rolling mountain road with gorgeous views.

In clear conditions, the view from the high ridges stretches over the entire city, and on rare winter days all the way to the ocean and Catalina Island. In summer, though, haze usually hangs over the basin. Wildfires have damaged this area repeatedly, and roads can close at short notice, so check the status before you set out.

Fuel is easy in Sierra Madre, Arcadia and Monrovia, and the area has a mix of old Californian diners and excellent Asian food, especially in Arcadia, which has a large Chinese American community and some of the best dumpling houses in the region. Go early on a weekday, and carry water on hot days.
t.death valley@33.9,-118.5:
The pin lands on the coast of Los Angeles near El Segundo and Manhattan Beach, within sight and sound of LAX, and the contrast with Death Valley, hundreds of kilometres to the northeast, is almost comic. After the heat, the dust and the silence of the desert, this is the city's edge: planes thundering in low over the beach, surfers in the water, and cyclists on the Strand, the paved path that runs along the sand.

El Segundo means the second in Spanish, and the town got its name in the early twentieth century when Standard Oil built its second California refinery here. The refinery is still working and its glowing towers at night add an industrial backdrop to the coast. Next to it lie the dunes of Dockweiler and Playa del Rey, where a small sandy preserve protects the El Segundo blue butterfly, a tiny insect found nowhere else. It is a strange thing to find at the end of a runway.

Manhattan Beach, a few kilometres south, is a polished beach town with a long pier, a lively volleyball scene and cafés full of people who look like they live on the sand. The sunsets here are excellent, and on clear evenings the sea turns to molten bronze. From here, Pacific Coast Highway runs south to the Palos Verdes peninsula, a rich, hilly district with ocean views, tight curves and cliffs, though the road is also crowded with cars and cyclists on weekends.

Traffic is the main hazard. Streets near the airport are choked in the late afternoon, lanes shift abruptly, and drivers are distracted. Allow plenty of time, and if you can, arrive after the evening peak. Everything is in easy reach: fuel, food, hotels, repair shops, car washes to rinse off the desert dust. There are fish tacos at stands along the coast, and the beach towns have a good range of coffee and bakeries.

Fog, known here as the June gloom, often blankets the coast in late spring and early summer, and the best weather comes in September and October. Ride out in the morning and enjoy the long, calm light on the water.
t.port de pollenca@39.9,3.1:
Port de Pollença is the seaside half of a partnership, with the old hill town of Pollença six kilometres inland. The port sits on a wide, sheltered bay in the north of Mallorca, with the Tramuntana mountains on one side and the Formentor peninsula curving round the other, and the water is calm, shallow and a clear green-blue. A long, pine-shaded promenade runs along the waterfront, lined with cafés and ice-cream shops, and sailing boats and fishing vessels bob in the harbour. It has about six thousand people in winter, and many more in summer, and it feels like a holiday town without being too brash.

The place has a long British connection, and you will hear English spoken in the cafés. Painters and writers came here in the early twentieth century, and the area has a quieter and slightly more refined atmosphere than the big resorts to the south. Up in Pollença, a famous stairway of 365 steps, the Calvari, climbs between cypress trees to a small chapel on the hill, and a Roman bridge crosses a dry stream bed. The old town's market on Sunday mornings fills the square with produce, cheese and crafts.

For riders, the port is the natural start of the road to Cap de Formentor. The ride begins gently along the bay and then climbs into pine forest, with views opening to the water and the cliffs, and from there it gets better and better. Both ends of the road are scenic, and the middle has the best bends. Plan the ride for the early morning, to beat the heat, the tour buses and the cyclists, who treat the road as a training run. Watch your speed through the villages and on the descent, where police occasionally check.

Fuel, supermarkets, bike shops and a wide choice of hotels are all available in the town, so this is the place to prepare. Evenings are lovely, when the sun goes down behind the mountains and the sky turns pink over the bay. Local food leans on seafood, with grilled fish, calamari and paella, and you should try a slice of ensaimada, the coiled sweet pastry of the island, with your coffee. The wind off the bay can be strong in the afternoons, particularly in spring.
t.puli@24.0,121.0:
Puli sits almost in the middle of Taiwan, in a basin ringed by the mountains of Nantou County, and people often call it the island's geographic heart. At the end of a long climb out of the high mountains, it is a relief: a town of about eighty-six thousand people with flat streets, warm air, and shops that stay open late. The elevation here is modest, so after the cold of the high passes the temperature feels like a gift.

The town is known for its water, which comes off the mountains clean and soft, and for the rice wine brewed with it, including Shaoxing wine that is sold across Taiwan and the sweet, fiery bottled versions that make good presents. The brewery has a visitor centre and an ice cream counter that sells rice wine ice cream, a combination which sounds odd and works well. The basin also produces bamboo shoots, tea, flowers and fruit, and the surrounding hills are dotted with temples and small farms.

The ride you are finishing is the Central Cross-Island Highway, one of the great mountain roads of East Asia. Built by army veterans in the 1950s, it crosses the island's spine from the Pacific coast to the west, passing through Taroko Gorge, where marble cliffs rise hundreds of metres, then climbs to the high ground at Wuling, which at about 3,275 metres is often described as the highest paved pass in East Asia.
